text: Swallow normally means to push food or drink down your throat. It also has a second use that has nothing to do with eating: to swallow a story or a piece of advice is to accept it without questioning it. The headline underneath the title uses that second meaning — parents took in bad advice about feeding children far too readily.

A fussy person is hard to please and complains about small things. Fussiest is the form meaning the most fussy of all. The article claims American children today are the fussiest eaters in history, which means no group of children before them turned down so much food.

Picky means choosing very carefully and rejecting most of what is offered — a picky eater will only eat a short list of foods. Helen Zoe Veit used the word as the one-word title of her book, which is why it keeps appearing in quotation marks here.

St Martin's Press is a book publisher — a company that turns an author's writing into printed books and sells them to shops. Reviews often print a line naming the publisher, the number of pages and the price, so a reader knows what they would be buying.

The United States Children's Bureau was an office of the national government, started in 1912, whose job was studying children's health and answering parents' questions about it. In 1915 an ordinary mother could write it a letter about her son and get a reply from an expert.

Federal means the national government, the one covering all the states at once rather than your town or state. That government is too big for one office, so it is divided into smaller offices called agencies, each given a single job and staffed by specialists. NASA and the Food and Drug Administration are two you may know; the Children's Bureau was another.

Maine is a state in the far north-east corner of the United States, up against Canada. Naming it signals that this was an ordinary family a long way from Washington, DC, writing in to the government for help.

Wholly means completely or entirely, with nothing held back. It is spelled from the word whole and sounds the same as holy, but the meanings are unrelated. The expert wholly dismissed the mother's idea, meaning he did not consider even a small part of it.

To dismiss can mean to send someone away, as when a teacher dismisses the class. Here it carries the other meaning: to reject an idea as not worth thinking about. The expert dismissed the suggestion that a boy might simply not like certain foods.

Voluntary means done by choice, because you decided to, rather than because something forced you. Voluntary food rejection therefore means a child turning food down on purpose — as opposed to being unable to eat it because of an illness, which is what the expert assumed was going on.

If something is unheard of, it never happens and nobody has ever come across it. The phrase is an exaggeration used for emphasis. Saying that voluntary food rejection was almost unheard of in 1915 means that children turning down dinner was so rare people barely had a name for it.

This is not the seconds on a clock. Asking for seconds means asking for a second helping of a meal — more of the same food, after your first plate is empty. It is a sign that a person is genuinely hungry and enjoying what they are eating.

Eat your heart out is a teasing phrase meaning roughly “be jealous”, usually aimed at someone who cannot have the good thing being described. The writer is joking with today's parents: children who ate whatever was served and asked for more are something modern parents can only envy. The food wording is a pun, since the whole article is about eating.

To decry something is to speak out against it publicly and say it is wrong or harmful. It is a stronger, more formal word than complain. Veit decries the changes in how adults think about feeding children, meaning her whole book argues against them.

A professor is a senior teacher and researcher at a university. Associate professor is a rank part-way up that ladder — above a beginning professor, below a full one. Mentioning it tells you the author studies this subject for a living rather than writing from personal opinion alone.

To hijack literally means to seize control of a vehicle, such as a plane or a truck, and force it to go where you want. People stretch the word to mean taking over anything and steering it off its normal course. Saying picky eating hijacked American childhood is a strong way of saying that fussiness took over the whole experience of growing up.

A century is a hundred years, and they are counted so that the number is always one ahead of the years themselves: the 20th century is the years 1900 to 1999, and we now live in the 21st. So before the 20th century means before about 1900.

Boundless means having no limit — no boundary where the thing stops. People use it for anything that seems to go on and on, like boundless energy or boundless curiosity. Children with boundless appetites would eat almost anything put in front of them and still want more.

Edith Wharton was an American novelist who lived from 1862 to 1937 and wrote about wealthy New York society. She is used here simply as evidence: she grew up before the 20th century and loved eating turtles and tiny crabs, foods most children today would refuse.

Mark Twain was the pen name of an American writer, Samuel Clemens, best known for the adventures of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn. He grew up in the 1840s, and his fond memories of huge childhood meals are used here as a second piece of evidence about how children once ate.

To extol something is to praise it warmly and at length. It is a formal word, usually used about things the speaker really admires. Twain extolled the meals of his childhood, meaning he wrote about them with obvious delight.

Sumptuous describes something grand and expensive-feeling, made without holding back. A sumptuous meal is large, rich and impressive rather than plain. The word sits in quotation marks because it is Twain's own description of what his family put on the table.

Venison is meat from a deer. Like beef from a cow or pork from a pig, it has its own name rather than being called deer meat. Venison just killed means it was eaten fresh, the same day it was hunted, which was normal before refrigerators.

An appetite is your desire to eat. To work up an appetite is to become properly hungry by going without food for a while or by being active. The article's point is that children once worked up appetites because they ate only at set mealtimes, with nothing in between.

A culprit is whoever, or whatever, is to blame for a problem. The word began as a term for a person accused of a crime and still works that way in a mystery story, but it is used just as often for a thing causing trouble. Snacking is named as one of the culprits behind fussy eating.

Someone finicky is very fussy about small details and hard to please, wanting things a particular way and refusing anything else. It can apply to food, handwriting or almost anything. Here it describes children who reject most of what is served to them.

To contend is to argue that something is true, especially when other people disagree. It signals a claim being made rather than a fact everyone accepts. When the article says the author contends, it is marking that idea as Veit's argument, not settled truth.

Whole foods are foods in close to their natural state — an apple, a potato, plain meat, milk — rather than foods broken apart and rebuilt in a factory with sugar, salt and flavourings added. The detail matters in the study described: children chose sensibly, but only because nothing else was on the table.

Devices here does not mean phones or tablets. To leave people to their own devices is to let them do as they please with no one directing them. The children in the study picked their own food with no adult telling them what to take.

Nutritious food is food that gives your body the substances it needs to grow and work properly — protein, vitamins, minerals and so on. A food can be filling without being nutritious. The study reported that children left alone still made nutritious choices.

To entrust someone with something is to hand it over to them because you trust them with it. It carries more weight than simply allowing. Spock's advice was that children should be entrusted with the decision about what and how much to eat, meaning adults should deliberately give up that control.

Autonomy is the power to make your own decisions without someone else deciding for you. It comes from Greek pieces meaning self and rule. Giving children more autonomy over food meant letting them choose their own meals instead of eating whatever was served.

Benjamin Spock was an American baby doctor whose 1946 guide to raising children became one of the best-selling books of the century. Millions of parents followed his advice, which is why a change in his thinking could change how a whole country fed its children.

Proliferation is rapid spreading — a quick increase in the number of something, or in how widely an idea travels. The proliferation of Freudian psychology means those ideas spread fast through books, doctors and ordinary conversation.

To popularise an idea is to take something known only to specialists and spread it to ordinary people, usually by explaining it in a simpler form. The Economist is British, so it spells the word with an s where American writing uses a z: popularized.

Psychology is the study of how minds work. Freudian psychology means the ideas of Sigmund Freud, an Austrian doctor of the early 1900s who taught that childhood experiences leave lasting marks on the adult mind. That teaching made parents afraid of causing harm at the dinner table.

A trauma is a deep injury, and traumatising someone means causing lasting harm to their mind, not a passing upset. It is a heavy word. Freudian thinking suggested that a mother pushing her child to eat a particular food might be doing that kind of damage.

Marie Antoinette was the queen of France who was executed during the French Revolution in 1793. The line often attached to her — that if the poor had no bread they should eat cake — was meant to show how far removed she was from ordinary people's lives.
A quip is a short, clever, usually witty remark. Calling the cake line a quip treats it as a throwaway one-liner rather than a serious statement of policy.

Placed before a noun like this, supposed means said to be true but not actually proven. Writers use it to keep their distance from a claim. Marie Antoinette's supposed quip signals that historians doubt she ever said it.

To contort something is to twist it out of its proper shape. It is normally used about bodies and faces, but an idea can be contorted too — bent until it means something quite different. The cake line was turned from a criticism of a selfish queen into an argument for giving children cake.

To underscore something is to emphasise it and make it stand out, the way drawing a line under a word does. Nothing is being written on here. The argument was that banning treats would underscore their value — forbidding cake makes cake seem like an even bigger prize.

Processed foods are foods changed in a factory before you buy them, usually broken down and rebuilt with sugar, salt, fat and flavourings added so they taste strong and last a long time. Breakfast cereal, crisps and packaged biscuits are examples. They are the opposite of the whole foods mentioned earlier.

A shop's stock is everything it keeps on hand to sell, so to say a supermarket stocked 7,000 items means it kept that many different products on its shelves. The number is a measure of choice: ten times as many different things to want as a shop of the 1920s held.

A target is what you aim at. In advertising, targeting means choosing which group of people an advertisement is meant to reach and then placing it where those people will see it. Targeting children directly meant putting the message in front of children themselves, even though their parents were the ones with the money.

Kellogg's is one of the largest American breakfast-cereal companies, the maker of corn flakes and many sugary cereals aimed at children. A remark from one of its advertising men carries weight because his company was among the first to aim at children directly.

To overrule someone is to cancel their decision using the authority you have over them. A referee can overrule an assistant; a parent can overrule a child. Veit's point is that adults already overrule small children about toothbrushing and seat belts without feeling guilty.

To buckle up is to fasten your seat belt — a buckle is the metal fastener that clicks shut. It is the everyday phrase for it in America. The article pairs it with toothbrushing as something adults simply insist on, no matter what a toddler says.

To venture somewhere is to go into it even though it is unfamiliar or slightly risky. Saying the author does not venture to other countries' food cultures means she never takes her book beyond America to look at how children eat elsewhere.

American exceptionalism is the idea that the United States is unlike any other country and follows its own path. Here it is used narrowly: the claim that American children became fussy in a way children elsewhere did not. The reviewer's complaint is that you cannot prove a country is unusual without looking at other countries.
Succinct means saying a lot in few words, with nothing wasted. It is praise when used about a book or a speech. The reviewer means the book makes its case without dragging on.

To digest food is to break it down so your body can use it. An easily digestible book is a joke built on that: one whose ideas go down easily and are not hard to take in. Reviewers of a book about eating enjoy ending on a food word.
